displayQuote: In this present crisis, government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem

meta.title: Who really said "In this present crisis, government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, Reagan said it — First Inaugural Address, 20 January 1981. But the famous short version deletes four words: "In this present crisis."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'In this present crisis, government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem'?
meta.ogDescription: Reagan really said it, in his 1981 inaugural. The version everyone quotes drops the opening clause that tied it to one economic crisis.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Reagan said it in his First Inaugural Address, delivered on the West Front of the U.S. Capitol on 20 January 1981, and the wording is confirmed sentence for sentence in the transcripts held by the Reagan Presidential Library ↗, the American Presidency Project ↗ and Yale’s Avalon Project ↗. What almost never survives the retelling are the first four words — “In this present crisis” — which tie the claim to the inflation and deficits he had just spent several paragraphs describing.

source.heading: Where the line comes from

docMeta.dd: 20 January 1981, West Front of the U.S. Capitol, Washington, D.C.
Ronald Reagan, 40th President of the United States
Kenneth Khachigian, Reagan’s chief White House speechwriter

source.excerpt: They will go away because we, as Americans, have the capacity now, as we have had in the past, to do whatever needs to be done to preserve this last and greatest bastion of freedom. In this present crisis, government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem. From time to time, we have been tempted to believe that society has become too complex to be managed by self-rule, that government by an elite group is superior to government for, by, and of the people.
trail: The Ronald Reagan Presidential Library ↗ transcript of the 20 January 1981 address carries the sentence with its opening clause intact, followed immediately by “From time to time we’ve been tempted to believe that society has become too complex to be managed by self-rule.”
The American Presidency Project ↗ and Yale Law School’s Avalon Project ↗ print the identical wording, placed directly after Reagan’s passage on inflation, unemployment and deficits.
Wikiquote ↗ lists the line in its sourced section for Reagan’s first term of office, citing the First Inaugural Address (1981).
Delivery is documented on film: the Library of Congress and GBH American Archive of Public Broadcasting ↗ hosts a broadcast clip of the passage from the 20 January 1981 coverage.
source.excerptNote: Later in the same speech Reagan added: “Now, so there will be no misunderstanding, it is not my intention to do away with government.”

source.rightsNote: The address is a work of the United States federal government, written and delivered in the President’s official capacity, so it carries no copyright in the United States — which is why full transcripts are published openly by the Reagan Presidential Library, Yale and Wikisource ↗, whose copy states that it “is in the public domain in the United States because it is a work of the United States federal government.” Note that this is public domain by the federal-works rule, not by age: a 1981 speech by a private citizen would still be in copyright.

author.name: Ronald Reagan
author.heading: About Ronald Reagan
author.bio: Ronald Reagan came to politics late, after a career as a sports broadcaster and Hollywood film actor and two stints as president of the Screen Actors Guild. He was governor of California from 1967 to 1975 and served as the 40th President of the United States from 1981 to 1989. He was a practised broadcaster long before he was a candidate, and built his politics around sentences designed to be repeated — which is precisely why this one travels so easily without its opening clause.

misattribution.heading: How the quote gets mangled
misattribution.intro: The attribution here is not in doubt — Reagan said these words, on the record, on camera. What goes wrong is the wording. The line is almost never quoted the way he actually delivered it.

items.who: “Government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem”
items.why: The opening clause “In this present crisis” is dropped so routinely that the Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation ↗ displays the shortened form on its own quotations page, attributed to the 1981 inaugural. Without those four words, a claim about one economic emergency reads as a permanent verdict on government itself.

items.who: “Government is not a solution to our problem…”
items.why: A widely reproduced variant swaps “the solution” for “a solution,” drops the opening clause, and cites no source document at all — as on AZQuotes ↗. Every archival transcript reads “the solution.”

items.who: Reagan, as a blanket anti-government slogan
items.why: Later in the very same address Reagan said: “Now, so there will be no misunderstanding, it is not my intention to do away with government.” Both sentences sit in the one speech, as the Avalon Project transcript ↗ shows.

misattribution.truthLine: The genuine sentence, from the Reagan Presidential Library transcript ↗ of 20 January 1981, is: “In this present crisis, government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem.”

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Reagan took the oath on 20 January 1981 on the West Front of the Capitol — the first inauguration held on that side of the building ↗. The address spent its opening minutes on inflation, idle factories and decades of deficits before it reached the sentence everyone remembers, and that sequence is the whole point: “this present crisis” had a specific referent sitting directly above it in the text.

The speech was drafted by Kenneth Khachigian, who wrote Reagan’s inaugural address ↗ and his early economic speeches as chief White House speechwriter. The same address promised to “curb the size and influence of the Federal establishment” and, a little further on, insisted that abolishing government was not the aim at all — a balance the shortened slogan cannot hold.
detailsBody: The crisis Reagan named was economic. The paragraphs immediately preceding the line describe “the longest and one of the worst sustained inflations in our national history,” idle industries casting workers into unemployment, and decades of piling “deficit upon deficit” — all readable in sequence in the Avalon Project transcript ↗. Read in place, the sentence is an argument about how to end stagflation rather than a general theory of the state.

None of this makes the short version a fabrication — Reagan did say the words that get quoted. It makes it an edit, and an edit that changes the scope of the claim from one emergency to all of government.
context.pull: “In this present crisis” — four words that turn a diagnosis into a doctrine the moment you delete them.
